Adding more days to this dataset

The dataset grows one weekday at a time. Pick a date and copy the request — the pipeline probes the archive for that day (holidays and ingestion gaps are rejected), fetches ~288 five-minute slices, merges them into the running aggregates, and this page is republished at the same address. Nothing recomputes from scratch: days already in are cached and stay in.

How speed is measured

Every bus reports its position about once a minute. For each consecutive pair of pings on the same journey we take the distance travelled over the time elapsed, then attribute that speed to the street the bus was on, matched by position and direction of travel.

This is door-to-door speed, including time spent stopped — at red lights, in traffic, and at bus stops. It is what a passenger on board actually experiences. The feed also carries its own instantaneous velocity reading, which runs about 9 km/h higher because it ignores every moment the bus is stationary.

What “bus-minutes lost” means

Each segment is compared against its own best hours, not against a city-wide target. A street's free-flow speed is the 85th percentile of its hourly medians — how fast buses move there when little is in the way. Stop spacing, turns and traffic lights are therefore already priced in.

Lost minutes are the delay against that baseline multiplied by how many buses actually pass: buses/hr × km × 60 × (1/v − 1/v_free). A slow street with two buses an hour scores low. A moderately slow street carrying sixty buses scores high — and that is where a bus lane pays for itself.

Reading it honestly

Position pings arrive roughly every 60 seconds, so a single reading spans 200–300 m of travel and is attributed to every block along its path. A block's colour is the median of many such crossings — robust, but neighbouring blocks share readings, so their values are not independent.

Time a bus spends parked at its origin before departure, and after it finishes its route, is stripped out — that is scheduled layover, not congestion. It accounted for of all readings.

Timed layovers mid-route, at large interchanges, are not stripped out — there is no signal in the feed that separates them from traffic. A segment beside a major terminal will therefore read slower than the traffic there alone would explain.

Corridor speed is total distance over total time, so a single jammed 200 m stretch pulls the whole corridor down instead of averaging away. That is deliberate: it is what the bus and its passengers feel.

Grey streets carry no scheduled bus we could observe. That is a genuine coverage gap on residential streets, but it is also the correct answer for service roads and slip lanes.

Freeways sit in the same ranking as high streets. Geha and Ayalon lose real bus-minutes, but the fix there is a shoulder lane or a ramp meter, not the kerbside bus lane a congested high street needs. Sort or filter by road class before drawing conclusions.
